newsitem.title: USA: Muni firm calls NASD criticism "utterly false".
newsitem.headline: Muni firm calls NASD criticism "utterly false".

text.p: Morgan Stanley on Tuesday said recent NASD criticism of its muni compliance procedures is wrong and it should not be barred from Massachusetts bond business for two years.

"NASDR's portrayal of Morgan Stanley's compliance procedures is utterly false," the firm said in a seven page brief to the Securities and Exchange Commission. The SEC is considering whether to hear the company's appeal of a February 1997 "pay-to-play" ruling effectively barring it from muni business for two years in Massachusetts.

NASD said in a June 9 brief that its decision to bar the firm from muni bond business in the state for two years was justified because of Morgan's sloppy procedures for complying with the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board's Rule G-37.

The pay-to-play rule bars muni dealers that make contributions to issuer clients from doing business for two years with the governments. NASD can grant exemptions from the rule using criteria developed by NASD and MSRB.
But Morgan Stanley shot back on Tuesday that NASD's protrayal is wrong. "Those briefs contain information that is factually and legally erroneous," the firm said.
Morgan Stanley added that while it wants to rebut the charges, it cannot because the arguments would have nothing to do with the SEC jurisdiction question.

The firm said NASD's decision denies it the opportunity to have its request thoroughly reviewed by SEC using five exemption factors set out under rule G-37. And it ultimately denies the firm the ability to do muni business in Massachusetts, the firm said.
Also, SEC must review the matter because it indirectly had a hand in the original denial decision, Morgan Stanley said.

In a 1996 Inspection Report, SEC told NASD not to grant exemptions in cases where a muni employee unwittingly makes a contribution, even if the firm repeatedly educated the person "and met all other requirements for granting an appeal."

"The SEC cannot instruct the NASDR regarding the standards it should use on Morgan Stanley and then not take jurisdiction to review that NASDR decision," the firm said in its brief prepared by Kenneth Gross, an attorney with Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom in Washington.
NASD Regulation, or NASDR, is the association's regulatory arm.
